title: Linux - Databases and Secret Material
html:
Databases and Secret Material on Linux Hosts

Database and application credentials often sit beside the service they support. Map the process, local socket or port, configuration, and credential file before testing whether an account can read data or execute a privileged operation.

Locate local data services and credentials

ss -lntup
ss -lnx
ps -eo user,pid,args | grep -E '[m]ysqld|[m]ariadbd|[p]ostgres|[r]edis-server|[m]ongod'
find /etc /opt /var/www /home -type f \( -name '*.env' -o -name '*config*' -o -name '.my.cnf' -o -name '.pgpass' \) -ls 2>/dev/null | head -100

Inspect readable application configs, deployment files, service environment files, and backups for connection strings or keys. A DB process's Unix socket can have different access rules from its TCP listener. Database permissions differ from OS permissions: a recovered DB password grants only the roles assigned to that DB account unless another path is demonstrated. In PostgreSQL, row-level security policies can hide records from one role while a role with policy-management rights can change that view; distinguish data access from policy administration. Use the service-specific guides for MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL, and Redis.

A readable automation script in another account's home may embed a credential even when its filename does not mention passwords. For example, a Python script can spawn su and pass a literal to its password prompt with pexpect.sendline; su still applies its authentication policy. Confirm that the current user can traverse the directory and read the exact script, that the literal is intended as the target account's password, and that the credential remains valid before treating it as an account transition. The script need not run successfully for its text to disclose a secret. Passive output should show the path and permissions without printing the value or trying a login.

A readable SQLite application database may contain user names and password hashes without any listening database service. Inspect its schema and file permissions before treating a hash as an offline audit lead. A recovered application password grants OS-account or local-admin-panel access only if reuse is separately confirmed; the hash format or matching user name is not proof of reuse.

Apache OFBiz can use an embedded Derby database under runtime/data/derby/<database>/. Derby's service.properties file marks the database directory; its sibling seg0 directory holds table files. Check permissions on the whole database directory before reviewing application records such as USER_LOGIN. A readable marker does not prove the tables are readable, that a password can be recovered, or that an application credential works for a Unix account. Keep database contents and password hashes out of routine enumeration output. See the Derby database-directory documentation and OFBiz login API.

TeamCity keeps its server data under a configurable data directory (often .BuildServer). Review permissions on config/projects/<project>/pluginData/ssh_keys, config/database.properties, system/buildserver.* when the embedded HSQLDB is used, and backup/TeamCity_Backup_*.zip. Uploaded SSH keys and other secure settings may be encrypted, so a readable path alone does not prove a usable private key. The database or backup can hold application users and password hashes; using them for a Unix account requires separate evidence of password reuse. Record paths and access rights during enumeration rather than printing keys, hashes, or database rows. See TeamCity's data-directory, SSH-key, and backup documentation.

The Duplicati backup server keeps configuration in Duplicati-server.sqlite. Its data directory may be under the service account's home, /var/lib/Duplicati, or a container volume, and --server-datafolder or DUPLICATI_HOME can change it. A readable database is a high-value lead because it can hold connection credentials and server signing material, but newer installations may encrypt sensitive fields and restrict directory access. Correlate its permissions with the actual server account and any authenticated UI or ServerUtil access. If that server runs as root with host / mounted into its container, authorized backup restore and job hooks can cross the host filesystem boundary; a loopback listener or database filename alone does not prove control. The nonce-based login behavior of older releases should not be assumed for current versions, which use a different authentication model. See Duplicati's server database and ServerUtil documentation for version-specific details.

For PostgreSQL, inspect pg_policies and pg_class.relrowsecurity to distinguish a filtered query from missing records. Changing or disabling a policy requires the appropriate table ownership or administrative privileges. A separately leaked maintenance account may have those privileges even when the application account does not. An unauthenticated Redis listener is another distinct finding: verify whether it binds only to loopback and whether protected mode or ACLs restrict the current connection before treating it as a secret source.

Review key and token stores

find /home /root -maxdepth 4 -type f \( -name 'id_*' -o -name '*.ppk' -o -name '*.p12' -o -name '*.pfx' -o -name '*.kdb' -o -name '*.kdbx' -o -name '*.gpg' -o -name '.git-credentials' \) -ls 2>/dev/null
find /home /root -maxdepth 4 -type d -name '.gnupg' -ls 2>/dev/null
printenv SSH_AUTH_SOCK KRB5CCNAME GNUPGHOME 2>/dev/null

An SSH private key, agent socket, Kerberos cache, GPG keyring, or PKCS#12 bundle is useful only if the current user can access it and any required passphrase or policy permits use. Inspect ownership and permissions first. The users and sessions, Linux AD, and post-exploitation pages explain the corresponding access paths. Git history, old backups, and shell history can also retain secrets after a live config has been cleaned. A readable .git directory can preserve deleted source and earlier committed credentials even when the working tree is empty; check access and review history manually rather than dumping it during automated enumeration.

A readable boot image under /boot is another archive lead. Initramfs boot scripts and copied helpers can include custom logic that supplies a key to cryptsetup --key-file=-. Check the image's access permissions and review only the relevant boot script and helper in an authorized offline copy. An embedded or derived disk-unlock passphrase is not automatically a Unix account password: confirm the helper's inputs, actual boot path, and separate credential reuse before treating it as an account transition. Routine enumeration should not unpack the image, execute its helpers, or print candidate keys.

The Vault CLI normally caches its authentication token in ~/.vault-token, although a custom token helper can store it elsewhere. A readable path is only a credential lead: verify token validity and policy before inferring access to any secret engine. For Vault SSH one-time passwords, the token must be authorized to issue credentials for a role whose user and CIDR include the intended account and host; that host must also have the SSH verification helper configured and accept the login. A role naming root or a token file alone does not prove root access. Passive enumeration should report the file path without reading the token or requesting an OTP.

KeePass 1.x uses .kdb, while KeePass 2.x uses .kdbx. Treat a matching filename as a possible encrypted vault, since other products may use the .kdb suffix. A readable vault does not reveal its entries without the required master password or key file; an SSH key stored as an attachment is a separate lead whose host access must be validated. KeePass accepts arbitrary files, including images, as key files, but a nearby file is only a candidate until its role, all required master-key components, and any higher-privileged account login are independently confirmed.

A support archive can contain both a KeePass vault and a process memory dump. For KeePass 2.x before 2.54, CVE-2023-32784 makes the master password potentially recoverable from a corresponding dump; an encrypted vault or unrelated dump alone is insufficient. Inspect archive entries and access rights manually without bulk extraction or printing secrets during routine enumeration. PuTTY private keys can appear as .ppk files or as PuTTY-User-Key-File text in a vault entry; confirm the key's intended account, encryption, and accepted host separately.

A readable .har HTTP archive can preserve browser requests and responses, including authentication headers, cookies, and form fields. It may be saved directly or inside a support attachment. Check ownership and access first, then inspect only the relevant entries; a filename alone does not prove a reusable credential. Automated enumeration should list the archive path without printing captured values. Microsoft Edge documentation explains the sensitive-data export option.

For encrypted database backups, correlate the readable archive, accessible private-key material, and any passphrase requirement before drawing a conclusion. Where authorized, recovery of a protected key's passphrase and inspection of decrypted backup data are separate manual steps. A database root credential is not a Unix root credential; password reuse across those accounts requires separate, authorized validation. Filesystem trust boundaries in web applications can also expose the account that owns these materials; see the Django file-cache review.

Container root and host root are separate identities. A private SSH key readable only after becoming root inside a container may authenticate to a host account if the host accepts it, but the key filename or public-key comment does not prove that access. Likewise, a custom password generator found beside a timestamped password-change record is only a manual analysis lead: a time-seeded non-cryptographic generator may have a small candidate seed window, but timezone, clock precision, library behavior, and later password changes affect reconstruction. Validate candidate credentials only when authorized; do not treat generated candidates as confirmed passwords.

A service account inside a container may be able to read an old provisioning script in a nominally privileged home directory if the directory is traversable and the file permissions allow it. An embedded application-admin password is a credential exposure lead, not host-root access: check whether the script and credential were active, which account the value belongs to, and whether a separate host account still accepts the same password. During passive enumeration, record the file path and access rights without printing the secret or attempting host authentication.

If a readable .p12 or .pfx bundle has a password exposed in application configuration, inspect it with openssl pkcs12 -info -in bundle.p12 -noout. Where the bundle contains an exportable private key, openssl pkcs12 -in bundle.p12 -nocerts -nodes -out extracted.key writes that key without encryption. Protect the output file and remove it after analysis; use the recovered key only for the service or ciphertext it actually matches. A bundle alone does not imply that its private key is useful for a different application.
